report_html:
Throw First, Ask Later

This is an aggressive, pass-leaning attack: +5% pass rate over expected, top of the league's range, and no interest in sitting on a lead (50% pass when ahead).

The Offensive Blueprint

There's no bell-cow to bank on — the lead back sees just 50% of carries (league ~59%), a committee that caps any one back's ceiling and makes their rushing props matchup- and script-dependent.

Travis Kelce is a genuine centerpiece, not an afterthought — 22% of targets (league ~15%).

They spread the ball as much as anyone — the WR1 commands only 16% of targets (league ~23%). Volume is democratic here, which suppresses any single receiver's ceiling but props up the TE and secondary options.

They live in the shotgun (80% of snaps vs ~68%) — a spread, pass-oriented structure.

When they fall behind they abandon the run entirely — 61% pass while trailing, so their pass-catchers have huge comeback-script ceilings.

Patrick Mahomes is a scramble threat — he takes off on 4.8% of dropbacks (nearly double the 3.3% norm), rushing production that both lifts his own yardage and siphons a few carries from the backfield.

By the numbers it's an efficient unit — a 46% success rate (above the 44% average).

In the Red Zone

Their red-zone identity is pass-first (56% pass), which puts scoring equity on Rashee Rice. And with the TE commanding 22% of targets, Travis Kelce is a live red-zone option too.

Defense — No Obvious Seam

They lock down opposing WR1s — just 50 rec yds/game (vs ~58); fade receiving props there.

They surrender 108 rushing and 220 passing yards per game (league ~120 / ~230). No dominant funnel — read it matchup by matchup.

The Betting Angles

Bottom line: Rashee Rice holds value even when they're winning; their pass-catchers have massive ceilings in comeback scripts (fade-material as underdogs).

Built on 2024–25 data; the profile rebuilds through the season as the current staff and roster set their own tendencies.
